title: Read in Daily Life: short texts
lines: Read in Daily Life uses the kind of English you will meet every day as a student abroad: notices on a door, a text from a classmate, a cafe menu, a bus timetable, a post in a campus group. The short version of the task gives you a text of about 25-80 words and two questions about it.
## What is on the screen
- The text appears on the left or top of the screen, often laid out like the real thing: a sign, a phone message, a small table or a social media post.
- Two multiple-choice questions follow, each with four options and one correct answer.

- Typical questions: What is the purpose of the notice? According to the message, what time does the event start? What does the phrase "on the house" mean? What should readers do if they want a refund?
## Timing

There is no separate timer for this task; it is part of the Reading module (about 30 minutes for all of Reading). Short texts should be quick points: aim for about 1 minute per text, including both questions. Time saved here is time you can spend on the academic passage.
## What is being tested
- Understanding the purpose of a practical text: to inform, to warn, to invite, to request, to advertise, to apologize.
- Finding a key detail quickly (a date, a price, a condition, a place).
- Understanding everyday phrases and abbreviations in context: "sold out", "while supplies last", "ASAP", "RSVP", "no later than".
- Working out what the reader is expected to do.
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: Look at the shape of the text first. Is it a sign, a message, a menu? Who wrote it and for whom? This takes two seconds and tells you the likely purpose.
- Step 2: Read the whole text once. It is short; reading the questions first saves very little here.
- Step 3: Read the first question and predict the answer before looking at the options.
- Step 4: Choose the option that matches your prediction in meaning, not in words. Correct answers usually paraphrase ("closed for repairs" becomes "temporarily unavailable").
- Step 5: For detail questions, go back and find the exact line. Check conditions such as "only", "except", "after", "before" and "unless".
- Step 6: For purpose questions, ask what the writer wants to happen. A notice that mentions a change in hours exists to inform people of the change, not to describe the building.
## Worked example 1
> Text message from Kwame: Hey, the study group is moving to Room 214 tonight, our usual room is booked for an exam. Same time, 7:00. Can you bring the extension cord? Mine is broken.
> Question: Why did Kwame send the message?
> A. To cancel tonight's study group
> B. To tell a friend about a change of location
> C. To ask a friend to repair an extension cord
> D. To invite a friend to take an exam

Predict first: the main news is the new room. B paraphrases "moving to Room 214". A is wrong because the meeting still happens ("same time"). C mixes two details: he asks his friend to bring a cord, and it is his own cord that is broken. D takes the word "exam" from the reason and builds a false idea around it.
> Question: What does Kwame ask his friend to do?
> A. Book a different room
> B. Arrive earlier than usual
> C. Bring an item to the meeting
> D. Lend him money for a new cord
C paraphrases "bring the extension cord" with a general word, "an item". B contradicts "same time", and A and D are not mentioned.
## Worked example 2
> Sign at a campus cafe: Hot breakfast served 7:30-10:30 a.m. weekdays only. After 10:30, sandwiches and salads are available until closing. Reusable cup? Take 25 cents off any drink.
> Question: What can be inferred about the cafe on Saturdays?
> A. It does not serve hot breakfast.
> B. It closes at 10:30 a.m.
> C. Drinks are cheaper than on weekdays.
> D. Only sandwiches are sold.

A is correct because hot breakfast is "weekdays only", and Saturday is not a weekday. B confuses the end of breakfast with closing time. C twists the cup discount, which has nothing to do with the day. D is too extreme: the sign says nothing about which other food is sold on Saturdays.
## Common traps
- Word-match options: an option that repeats a striking word from the text ("exam", "broken") but changes the meaning.
- Mixing two details: the right people, the wrong action; the right time, the wrong day.
- Too extreme: "always", "never", "only", "all" when the text is less absolute.
- True but not the answer: a fact from the text that does not answer this question.
- Missing small words that change the meaning: "no later than Friday" means Friday or earlier; "except Sundays" removes a day.
! In purpose questions, the first line often states the news and the rest gives details. Do not choose a detail as the purpose.
## Everyday language to know
- Notices: until further notice, closed for maintenance, out of order, staff only, by appointment only.
- Shopping and food: on sale, sold out, while supplies last, complimentary, on the house, gluten-free, take-out.
- Messages: running late, heads up, can you cover for me, let me know, no worries, ASAP.
- Deadlines: due by, no later than, at the latest, extended to, postponed until.
## How to practise between mocks
- Read real everyday English: shop signs in English, bus and train timetables, product labels, university web pages and student union notices.
- For every text you read, say in one sentence who wrote it, why, and what the reader should do.
- Collect phrases that have a special meaning in notices (such as "until further notice") in a notebook with an example.
- In practice sets, write down why each wrong option is wrong; you will start to see the same four or five trap types again and again.
- Work on speed: time yourself on sets of short texts and try to keep to about one minute each without losing accuracy.
